Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette:
Keoni sat in the clinic waiting room with his hands pressed flat on his thighs, trying not to look at the door every time it opened. At sixty-three, he had spent most of his adult life moving through crowded community meetings, standing at podiums, talking face-to-face with neighbors about zoning laws and school funding. Now the simplest interaction-someone raising their voice to make a point, even calmly-sent a wash of heat up his neck and made his chest tighten as if he were about to be struck. He had no idea how to explain that to the therapist.

The accident happened three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in late spring. Keoni had been driving home from a neighborhood coalition meeting, tired but satisfied. At a four-way intersection, a truck ran the red light and T-boned his sedan. The impact spun the car into a utility pole. What Keoni remembered with excruciating clarity was the sound-metal tearing, glass exploding-and then the face of the other driver, a man in a deputy sheriff's uniform, who got out of the truck and started shouting. The man was furious, yelling that Keoni had come out of nowhere, that it was his fault. In that moment, Keoni could not speak. He could not move. His left arm was broken, his ribs cracked, and he was bleeding internally, but what stayed with him was the rage in the other man's voice and the insignia on his collar. Other parts of the crash were simply gone. He could not remember the seconds before impact no matter how hard he tried. He knew he had seen the truck coming, but the memory would not come. When he tried to tell his sister about it later, the words would not form. He knew what had happened, but his mouth would not cooperate; he could only gesture and shake his head.

In the weeks that followed, Keoni told himself the accident was his fault. If he had looked left one more time, if he had slowed down, if he had not been so tired, the truck would have missed him. That thought looped daily, even though the police report placed blame on the other driver. But there were also unwanted thoughts that came out of nowhere, unbidden-not triggered by a sound or a sight, just floating into his mind while he washed dishes or sat on the couch. He would suddenly see the deputy's contorted face, or hear his own heartbeat roaring in his ears, or feel the sickening jolt of the impact, and his chest would seize up before he could stop it. He began to notice that his body did not believe he was safe. At home, alone in his small apartment (his divorce had been final for a decade), he would hear a car horn outside and find himself on the floor, heart hammering, before he knew what he was doing. He had come to believe that his own body was his enemy, that it kept reacting as if the crash were still happening, that it would betray him at any moment. And underneath that was a deadness he could not shake. He felt hollow, numb, as if something vital inside him had been scooped out.

The triggers narrowed his world. At community meetings, which used to be his lifeblood, someone would express frustration about a pothole or a broken streetlight, and Keoni would see the deputy's face again, hear that tone, and his mind would blank. He stopped attending. He dodged phone calls from colleagues. He took different routes to the grocery store to avoid passing the sheriff's substation. The sight of a uniform-any uniform, even a security guard at the mall-made his stomach drop. His work as a community organizer had always depended on his presence, his voice, his willingness to sit with anger and turn it into action. Now anger itself, even when it was calm and directed elsewhere, felt like a threat. His absence became noticeable. A coalition he had helped build for fifteen years lost momentum without him. His colleagues assumed he was sick or burned out. He could not correct them because he could not find the words.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a single moment. A young mother he had mentored for years called him, asking for help with a school board issue. She said she needed him, and he heard the frustration in her voice-not angry, just urgent-and he hung up. Then he sat in his kitchen and wept. The next morning he called his primary care doctor and asked for a referral. He did not know if talking would make the unwanted thoughts stop or if it would only give them more room to crowd in. He did not know if he could describe the accident at all. But he knew he could not keep watching his life shrink into the space between his couch and his front door. What he hoped most was to feel something again, even if it hurt. What he feared most was that the numbness was all that was left.
